title: Chapter 17: Ade Goes In After Her
content: Rain since four on Thursday. The river up eight inches by six.

It comes off the cannery roof in sheets and stands in the gravel at the bottom of the ramp. The ramp goes under at the second step. Wren stands in it to her ankles with one hand on the gunwale and the other on the bow line, and the water is colder than it was on Sunday, and that is the first sign.

Eleven people wait on the west bank under the diner awning and the hardware store awning, and the awnings are not enough, and nobody in this town owns an umbrella, because nobody in this town has needed one since 1998.

The first four go at ten past six. The Pruitt brothers off the cannery line, a woman with a grocery bag held against her chest inside her coat, and a man with a cast on his wrist who holds it up out of the rain like a lamp.
The crossing takes eleven minutes, which is slow. The water is pushing from the north now and she has to angle harder, and twice the bow comes around and she has to fight it back with the oar.
She comes back at twenty-four past six.
Nine.
Nine people on the ramp, standing in the rain, and the rain is coming down so hard that they are not so much standing in it as under it.
Ade counts them with his finger, out loud, the way he counts everything, the way he has counted every load since Friday.
"Nine."
"I see nine."
"Four is the rule."
"I know the rule."

The river has come up three inches in the last hour, and in forty minutes the water will be up another six and the light will be gone, and the piling will be a foot under and invisible, and the rain will be worse.
She can hear the piling from here. It makes a small round suck in the current, a sound like a drain.
"One trip," she says.
Ade looks at the water. Then at the nine. Then at her.
"Two," he says.
"One."
"Wren."
"One trip, and we go wide of the piling, and we are all on the east bank in nine minutes." She takes the bow line off the post. "Two trips is forty minutes in the dark. One trip is nine."
"It is nine people in a fourteen-foot boat."
"It is nine people in a fourteen-foot boat for nine minutes."

He does not argue. He never argues with her in front of passengers. He takes the lantern and puts it in the bow and stands in the water holding the boat, and his jaw is set in the way it gets, and that is the whole of his objection.
Junie Hale goes in the bow because her mother puts her there and because the bow is the dry end.

Junie is six. Red boots, a coat with a hood that has gone flat, a plastic horse in her fist. She sits where she is put and she does not cry. Frances Hale gets in behind her daughter and puts one hand on the back of her neck.

The Pruitt brothers take the middle bench, one on each side, and Dale Fisk, seventy-one, sits between them with his hands on his knees. Nell Acker gets in with her grocery bag and sets it on the floor between her feet. Curtis Boone, cast and all, takes the port side. The two teenagers, a girl and a boy, get in last of the passengers and hold hands on the stern bench and do not look at anybody.
Nine. The gunwale is four inches above the water when they are all in, and the boat sits low and heavy and does not want to turn.
Ade coils the bow line over his shoulder and steps in over the stern, and there is no room to sit, so he stands.
He puts his hand on the top of Junie's hood, once, the way you would touch a dog.
"Six thirty-one," Wren says, for the book, and pushes off.

The rain is not rain now. It is water in the air, all of it at once, and the lantern makes a yellow fog she cannot see through. She rows by the shape of the far bank and by memory, and the memory is a light on a shed and a gravel ramp and a fence.
The river is loud. It is louder than the rain, and the rain is loud, and under it there is the sound the water makes going through the piling: that suck, that drain.
Halfway across, the wind comes out of the north.

Not a gust. A wall. The kind of thing that takes a hat off a man and puts it in the next county. It hits the boat broadside and the lantern swings and the rain goes sideways and for a second the far bank disappears.
Then the wave comes behind it.
It is not a wave. It is the river standing up. Four feet of black water with a white top, moving faster than the boat, and it hits the bow and comes over.
The boat drops. The bow goes under and comes up throwing water. The lantern goes out.
Junie Hale is in the water.

Nobody screams. That is the thing Wren will remember. The child does not scream and neither does her mother. There is a sound like a door closing, and then there is water, and then there is Ade going over the side without a word.
He has the bow line in his hand. The line runs out behind him like a tail and then it is in the water with him.
Wren has one oar. She puts it in and pulls, and the boat comes around, and the current takes the stern and swings it, and she sees the piling.
Too late.

The hull hits the steel collar and the sound goes up through her arms and into her teeth. The boat rolls. Water comes over the port side and Nell Acker goes down on her knees and the boy screams, finally, one long note.
Wren gets the oar in the water and holds. The boat scrapes along the collar, metal on metal, and comes free.
Twenty feet downstream, in the dark, there is a light.
The lantern. It is under the water, still burning, a yellow coin going down, and it lights the underside of the river for one second and then it is gone.
In that second she sees Ade's arm.
He has Junie by the back of her coat. He is holding her up out of the water with both hands, the way a man holds a sack of feed, and the child's red boots are kicking.
Wren puts the boat at them.
"Here. Here. Here."
She says it three times, flat, and the third time is a shout.

Ade gets a hand on the gunwale. The boat goes down with his weight and water comes over the rail. He shoves Junie up, and Wren has her by the hood, then by the collar, then by the arm, and she pulls her over the side and the child lands in the bottom of the boat like a wet coat.
Ade's other hand comes up. She takes it.
His hand is cold. It is the coldest thing she has ever touched. It is a hand that has been in the river.
She has him by the wrist and she is pulling, and the boat is rolling, and the rain is going sideways, and then the bow line comes tight.
The line is still over his shoulder. The other end is fouled on the piling.
The current takes the bow around and the line comes taut and it pulls him back, and his hand comes out of hers.
He goes under.
The line runs out. Then it goes slack.
She looks at the water for four seconds. She counts them. She will count them for the rest of her life.

There are nine people in the boat and the boat is full of water to the second bench. Nell Acker is bailing with her hands. Dale Fisk has the teenager girl by the collar of her coat. Frances Hale has her daughter against her chest with her mouth open and no sound coming out of it.
If she goes in, the boat goes.
She puts the oar in the water.
She rows with one oar. She sculls, which is what you do when your oar has gone and the river is taking you, and it is slow and ugly and it works.
Two hundred yards takes four minutes.
She beaches on the gravel two hundred yards below the shed. The bow grinds. Nobody moves.
"Out," she says. "Everybody out. Up the ramp."
They get out. She counts them with her finger the way he counts.
Nine.
She counts again. Nine.
Then she runs.

Up the ramp, along the bank, back down through the gap in the fence with the flashlight, calling his name, and the rain takes the name out of her mouth and puts it in the water. She wades to her waist at the piling and puts her hands down in the dark and feels the collar, and the concrete, and something soft that turns out to be a grocery bag.
She calls until her voice is gone. Then she calls without her voice.

Ruthie is at the top of the ramp in her apron with no coat on. Mars comes at seven twenty with the county radio in her hand and gets the volunteer boat out of Marietta, and the deputy comes at seven forty, and the fire boat comes from the west bank at eight fifteen with a light bar and a drag.
They drag until one in the morning.

The chief is a man named Dorn who has known her since she was a child. He takes his helmet off to talk to her, which is what they do, and he says they will be back at first light, and he says the word recovery, and she hates him for it and understands it.
She takes the boat out herself at nine thirty and works the piling with a grappling hook for two hours. The hook comes up with a coat on it. The coat is not his.
At one in the morning Mars drives her up to the house and makes her eat half a sandwich and sits with her until she stops shaking.
The rain stops at five.
She is on the step with a blanket around her when the light comes up, and the river is brown and high and going past like a train, and there is a tree in it, whole, with the roots up.
She walks the gravel.
She finds the boot forty feet below the shed, right side up, full of water, one lace gone.
A boot does not float. A boot fills and sinks and the river rolls it along the bottom and puts it down somewhere, and this one is on the gravel in the shallows like it was set there.
She tips it and the water comes out, and there is a sock in it, and the sock is his.
She carries it up the ramp and sets it by the door beside the other one, which has been there since six thirty-one last night, and now they are a pair again.
Only one of them is wet.
highlight: Rain, a standing wave, and Ade Kessler goes into the water after a child and does not come up.
